newsitem.title: USA: GM to sell Hughes defense assets to Raytheon.
newsitem.headline: GM to sell Hughes defense assets to Raytheon.

text.p: General Motors Corp.'s Hughes Aircraft defence subsidiary will be sold to Raytheon Co. in a deal valued at $9.5 billion, the automaker announced Thursday.
The announcement made Raytheon the winner in a bidding war with Northrop Grumman Corp.
The purchase price consists of $5.1 billion in Raytheon stock and $4.4 billion in debt, Raytheon said.
The Hughes defence unit -- which makes missiles, radar equipment and other defence electronics -- was a highly valued prize in the rapidly consolidating defence industry.

The merged Raytheon-Hughes company, which will retain the Raytheon name, will probably create the third largest U.S. defence contractor after the combination of Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp., which have agreed to merge, and Lockheed Martin Corp.
"We are truly creating another defence electronics powerhouse," Raytheon Chairman Dennis Picard said in a statment.
Raytheon also makes missiles, including the Patriot air defence missile, radar, and communications and air traffic control systems. It also makes Amana appliances and Beech aircraft.
GM Chairman Jack Smith said the deal was aimed at unlocking value for GM shareholders and was a response to "the rapidly changing landscape in the defence industry."
"The spin-off of Hughes Aircraft and its merger with Raytheon optimize the value that all holders of GM common stock can realise from this valuable asset."

The Hughes defence units posted 1995 operating earnings of $688 million on revenues of about $6 billion. GM bought El Segundo, Calif.-based Hughes for about $5 billion in 1985 in a controversial deal engineered by then-chairman Roger Smith.
Raytheon estimated the merged company's combined annual revenues at about $21 billion and said it would have 127,000 employees.

GM said the deal did not include other assets of its Hughes Electronics Corp. unit. The automaker is retaining Hughes' lucrative telecommunications and space unit, which builds satellites and operates the fast-growing DirecTV satellite broadcasting service.
Hughes Chairman C. Michael Armstrong will continue to run the remaining Hughes Electronics businesses.

GM also plans to move Hughes' Delco Electronics, its automotive electronics business, back into its Delphi Autmotive Systems parts operation. Smith, speaking at a news conference in New York, said GM will consider a future public offering or spin-off of the new Delphi-Delco unit.
The complicated transaction contains several steps:
-- Hughes Aircraft will take on about $3.7 billion to $4.7 billion in new debt, which will primarily be injected into the telecommunications and space business that GM is keeping.

-- GM will effect a tax-free spinoff of Hughes Aircraft to holders of GM's Class H and $1-2/3 par value, or automotive, common stock. The distribution will give GM common shareholders control of about 30 percent of the merged Raytheon-Hughes common stock.

-- Hughes Aircraft will then merge with Raytheon. GM values the transaction at $9.5 billion, including the $4.7 billion in Hughes Aircraft debt and $4.8 billion worth of Hughes Aircraft stock to be distriubted to shareholders.
-- GM will recapitalize its Class H stock to link it solely to the telecommunications and space business. Earnings associated with Delco Electronics will be reallocated to GM's main automotive stock.

"In the past we have felt the market imposed a conglomerate discount to Class H stock because it tracked three businesses," Smith told reporters. "Now the recapitalized Class H stock will track only one high-growth area, telecommunications."

GM officials boasted that DirecTV, which uses an 18-inch satellite dish, was off to the biggest start of any consumer electroncs product in history, eclipsing the early years of the colour television set and videocassette recorder.
DirecTV has about 2.3 million subscribers in the United States and expects growth of 20 percent per year over the next several years.
